CausalChain: DDR gene alterations in BTC -> increased genomic instability and neoantigen formation -> partial immune activation countered by an immunosuppressive TME (e.g., PD-L1, Tregs, MDSCs) -> DDR inhibitors further activate cytosolic DNA sensing (STING pathway) releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines -> Advanced, biomarker-guided TME modulators reprogram the immune-suppressive niche -> synergistic effect sensitizes BTC tumors to immune checkpoint blockade
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancer, tumors with DDR pathway deficiencies, despite exhibiting low MSI and moderate TMB, can be rendered more immunoresponsive by a dual therapeutic strategy that combines DDR inhibitors (e.g., PARP inhibitors) with TME-targeting agents identified through contemporary digital and multi-omics technologies (including single-cell sequencing and AI-assisted biomarker discovery). This combination amplifies neoantigen formation and STING-mediated inflammatory signaling while simultaneously reconfiguring the immunosuppressive TME, ultimately enhancing neoantigen-driven immune activation and improving the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Abstract: We hypothesize that a precision, dual-therapy approach can transform immunologically “cold” biliary tract cancers (BTCs) into responsive tumors by leveraging DDR pathway deficiencies. Specifically, in BTC tumors that exhibit low microsatellite instability (MSI) and moderate tumor mutational burden (TMB), pharmacological inhibition of DDR pathways (e.g., PARP inhibitors) can exacerbate genomic instability and neoantigen generation while concurrently activating the STING pathway. However, the inherent immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) restricts this effect. By integrating targeted TME modulators—selected through advanced multi-omics profiling, single-cell sequencing, and imaging-guided biomarker analysis—with DDR inhibitors, we propose that the enhanced neoantigen landscape can be effectively exploited to restore robust immune surveillance. This refined hypothesis combines mechanistic insights with contemporary technological advances to improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in BTC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that DDR deficiencies in BTC could be targeted by combining DDR inhibitors with TME modulators to potentiate immunotherapy responses by enhancing neoantigen presentation. The revised hypothesis retains the core idea of exploiting DDR-induced genomic instability and neoantigen formation but incorporates advanced technological innovations such as multi-omics profiling, single-cell sequencing, and AI-assisted biomarker discovery to better identify and modulate the immunosuppressive TME. Each causal step is addressed: (1) DDR alterations lead to genomic instability and neoantigen generation; (2) the generated neoantigens are insufficient alone due to TME suppression; (3) DDR inhibitors activate the STING pathway yet are hampered by the TME; and (4) integration with modern, targeted TME modulators reprograms the microenvironment to fully engage immune surveillance and sensitize tumors to checkpoint inhibitors.
